sec.title: Introduction and aims
sec.p: Understanding the identity of odontogenic cells is fundamental to advancing research in tooth development and regeneration. We aim to explore the cellular composition, differentiation pathways, and regulatory networks in human embryonic teeth during the transition from the cap stage to the early bell stage.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The spatial RNA sequencing and single-nucleus RNA sequencing to human embryonic tooth germs were obtained from four healthy aborted specimens and integrated with public database. The spatial and temporal gene expression patterns, cell distributions, and interactions in tooth germ and surrounding periodontal tissues spanning postconception weeks 12 to 18 were examined and validated by immunohistochemistry.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Our analysis identified diverse cell types, including 10 epithelial and nine mesenchymal subpopulations, alongside smooth muscle cells, endothelial cells, macrophages, and Schwann cells. We characterized epithelial and mesenchymal lineages by defining their signature genes, regulatory transcription factors, spatial distributions, and differentiation trajectories, while revealing conserved and distinct features between oral and odontogenic cells. Developmental stage-specific intercellular communications were delineated for epithelial and mesenchymal compartments. Notably, SPP1+ macrophages mediated crosstalk with odontoblasts via SPP1-integrin receptor interactions, whereas Schwann cells contributed to the signalling landscape via SEMA3C/MDK/PDGFC ligands.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This study reveals the cellular heterogeneity present in human embryonic teeth during early development, identifies key genes governing the differentiation of epithelial and mesenchymal cells, and provides valuable transcriptomic resources for investigating human embryonic tooth development.

sec.title: Clinical relevance
sec.p: Characterizing cells into more precise subgroups will enhance the potential to select optimal cell types for regenerative applications. The characteristic genes in differentiated cells could serve as potential inducers to guide the directed differentiation of stem cells.
Key words: Human embryonic teeth, Spatial RNA sequencing, Single-nucleus RNA sequencing, Spatial-temporal expression pattern
Collection date 2025 Dec.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Teeth serve as an excellent model for studying organ development, particularly for investigating epithelial-mesenchymal interactions, cell differentiation, and tissue mineralization.1 During embryogenesis, odontogenic stem cells exhibit strong self-renewal capacity and the ability to differentiate into multiple lineages. These characteristics offer promising avenues for advancing research in tooth development and regenerative dentistry. Traditionally, odontogenic cells have been identified using various dental markers such as dentin sialophosphoprotein (DSPP), alkaline phosphatase, mineralized nodules, and type I collagen.2 However, isolating and precisely locating these cells remains a significant challenge. Gaining a deeper understanding of their biological characteristics during the embryonic phase may improve strategies for their identification and isolation, enabling more reliable experimental approaches.

The emergence of multiomics technologies has significantly deepened our understanding of natural tooth development. By establishing single-cell transcriptomic atlases of human and mouse teeth, researchers have identified cellular heterogeneity, differentiation mechanisms, and epithelial-mesenchymal crosstalk.3,4 Furthermore, spatial transcriptomic technologies enable gene expression profiling of specific tissue locations using spatial coordinates. Recently, integrated single-cell RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and spatial RNA-seq analyses have been employed to construct reference landscapes of human teeth spanning postconception weeks 9 (PCW9) to PCW24.5, 6, 7 However, the paucity of spatial transcriptomic data limits the continuous investigation of early human tooth development.

To investigate the development of human embryonic teeth and their surrounding tissues, we integrated public databases with our in-house single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq) and spatial RNA-seq data from the cap-to-early bell stage (PCW12-PCW18). This integrated approach allowed us to chart spatial-temporal gene expression patterns, trace differentiation trajectories of odontogenic cells, and explore intercellular communication within the periodontal niche. Furthermore, this study supplements transcriptomic data related to oral development under natural conditions.

sec.title: Sample collection
sec.p: This study utilized healthy human embryonic tooth samples at developmental stages PCW15 and PCW18 for snRNA-seq, with each sample providing two mandibular molars. Additionally, mandibular tissue samples at PCW12 and PCW15 were used for spatial RNA-seq. All specimens were collected following elective medical terminations from pregnancies with no detectable abnormalities. Clinical ultrasound was employed to exclude conditions such as congenital heart disease and cleft lip or palate. Noninvasive prenatal screening and chromosomal microarray analysis were also used to rule out chromosomal aneuploidy and pathogenic genetic mutations. Developmental age was estimated through clinical ultrasound and verified by histological examination (Figure S1A).

sec.title: SnRNA-seq data preprocessing
sec.p: Library quality control, alignment, and gene count generation were performed using Cell Ranger. Cells with fewer than 1000 unique molecular identifiers, fewer than 200 or more than 20,000 genes, or mitochondrial gene content exceeding 5% were excluded using Seurat. RNA contamination and doublets were filtered using SoupX and Scrublet, respectively. Data were log-normalized and integrated using the top 2000 highly variable genes and the first 20 principal components. Cell cycle regression was applied via Seurat, and batch effects were corrected using Harmony. Dimensionality reduction was performed using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP). All the package versions were provided in Supplementary Materials.

Public datasets (GEO accession GSE184749) from the sci-RNA-seq platform, including embryonic molars and incisors at PCW12 to 13, PCW14 to 16, and PCW17 to 19, were incorporated for comparative analysis. For clarity, we refer to these as PCW12, PCW15, and PCW18 throughout the manuscript.

sec.title: Spatial RNA-seq data processing
sec.p: Space Range was used for alignment and data filtering. Cells with fewer than 200 or more than 2500 detected genes or >5% mitochondrial gene content were excluded. Normalization was performed using Seurat’s SCTransform function. Spatial transcriptomic data were processed following the same filtration criteria as snRNA-seq.

sec.title: Cell type identification
sec.p: Marker genes were identified using Seurat’s FindAllMarkers function, applying the following thresholds: adjusted P value <.05, |log₂(fold change)| ≥0.25, and pct.1 to pct.2 ≥0.25. Pseudobulk analysis and DESeq2 were also used to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs), with a stricter threshold of |log₂(fold change)| ≥1. Cell identities were assigned based on published scRNA-seq tooth datasets and marker gene scoring using the AddModuleScore function. Functional annotation of clusters was performed using clusterProfiler and Metascape.8

sec.title: SnRNA-seq data analysis
sec.p: Transcription factor (TF) regulatory networks were inferred using pySCENIC, referencing hg38 gene annotations within a ±10 kb window. The AUCell module was used to assess regulon activity in each cell population. Differentiation trajectories were reconstructed using Monocle3, and cellular entropy was calculated using SLICE to assess differentiation potential.9 RNA velocity was analysed using velocyto. Cell–cell communication analysis was conducted using CellChat, focusing on secreted ligand-receptor interactions.

To compare human and mouse datasets, we performed Pearson correlation analysis with publicly available mouse scRNA-seq data (GSE131204, GSE162413, GSE189381). Visualization was achieved using R packages including ggplot2, ComplexHeatmap, and scRNAtoolVis. Cell cycle scoring was carried out with tricycle, and similarity scoring between epithelial and mesenchymal subtypes was calculated using CARD.10

sec.title: Spatial RNA-seq data analysis
sec.p: Using annotations from snRNA-seq, spatial deconvolution was performed using RCTD.11 Gene spatial distributions were visualized using SPATA2. Spatial distances between odontogenic and periodontal cells were analysed using CellTrek. Ligand-receptor interaction networks were further evaluated with SpaGene and CellChat.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses were conducted using R. For multigroup comparisons, one-way ANOVA with FDR correction (<0.05) was used. Two-group comparisons were assessed via Student’s t test and fold-change analysis. Correlations were calculated using Pearson’s coefficient.

sec.title: A single-cell atlas of human embryonic teeth from the cap to early bell stage
sec.p: To identify key markers of odontogenic cells in human embryonic teeth, we performed snRNA-seq on mandibular molars at PCW15 and PCW18, along with spatial RNA-seq on mandibular tissues at PCW12 and PCW15. These samples were obtained from four independent human specimens. Additionally, we incorporated publicly available datasets spanning PCW12 to 13, PCW14 to 16, and PCW17 to 19, covering both embryonic molars and incisors. After rigorous quality control – including removal of RNA contamination, doublets, and batch effects – a total of 26,394 high-quality cells were retained for snRNA-seq analysis: 3411 cells at PCW12, 9931 at PCW15, and 13,052 at PCW18. For spatial transcriptomics, 1010 cells at PCW12 and 2145 cells at PCW15 were analysed. Quality control metrics are provided in Figure S1B to F.

Using the FindClusters function with a resolution of 0.9, we identified 21 distinct cell clusters. These were categorized into five major cell types: epithelial cells (KRT14+/PITX2+), mesenchymal cells (MSX1+/PRRX1+), endothelial cells (PECAM1+/VWF+), immune cells (PTPRC+), and Schwann cells (PLP1+/CDH19+), forming 18 core subpopulations. Clusters 3, 19, and 20, which expressed mixed markers from multiple lineages, were excluded from further analysis (Figure 1A and Figure S1G). Cell composition analysis showed a predominance of epithelial and mesenchymal cells, with a noticeable increase in immune cells across developmental stages (Figure 1B). Notably, samples from our dataset showed higher proportions of immune and Schwann cells compared to those generated using the sci-RNA-seq platform.

caption.p: Spatial-temporal patterns of odontogenic cells during human embryonic tooth development (cap-to-early bell stage). (A) UMAP plots showing cell clustering by type, subpopulation, and developmental stage. (B) Cell type proportions across developmental stages and sequencing platforms. (C) Spatial mapping of annotated cell types in tissue sections at PCW12 (top) and PCW15 (bottom). Scale bar: 200 μm.

sec.p: Using cell annotations derived from snRNA-seq, we projected the spatial distribution of each cell type (Figure 1C). Endothelial cells were localized primarily within the submucosal layer, while immune and Schwann cells were dispersed along vascular regions. The localization patterns of epithelial and mesenchymal cells aligned well with tissue morphology. Key marker genes – KRT14 for epithelial cells, SCUBE3 for dental-specific markers, and TFAP2B for mesenchymal cells – further confirmed these spatial patterns (Figure S1H). Together, these data outline a preliminary spatial-temporal cell atlas of human embryonic tooth development from the cap to early bell stage.

sec.title: Molecular features of odontogenic epithelial cells from cap to early bell stage
sec.p: To explore the heterogeneity among odontogenic epithelial cells, we isolated KRT14+/PITX2+ cells and classified them into 10 distinct subtypes (Figure 2A,B, Table S1). Clusters 0 and 5, expressing the stem cell marker SOX2, were identified as stem/progenitor cells.12 Among these, dental epithelial stem cells (Dental epi) displayed elevated expression of KRT5 and KRT17. In contrast, oral epithelial basal/suprabasal cells (Oral epi basal) expressed keratinocyte differentiation genes including KRTDAP and MEIS2. Functional enrichment indicated that genes in Dental epi cells were linked to neuronal signalling and Rho GTPase pathways, whereas those in Oral epi basal cells were involved in epidermal development.

(B) Heatmap of key marker genes distinguishing each epithelial subtype. (C) Comparison of marker gene expression between dental and oral epithelial cells. (D) Spatial expression of MPPED1 (dental marker) and KRTDAP (oral marker). (E) Spatial localization of epithelial subpopulations using cell deconvolution. Scale bar: 200 μm. (F) Proportions of epithelial subpopulations across developmental stages. (G) Cell cycle phase distribution in epithelial subpopulations. (H) Key transcription factors identified in epithelial subpopulations. (I) Differential gene expression and pathway enrichment using pseudobulk analysis; labelled DEGs are conserved in both human and mouse datasets. (J) Correlation of epithelial subpopulations between human and postnatal mouse teeth. Dental epi, dental epithelial stem cells; IEE, inner enamel epithelium; OEE, outer enamel epithelium; Oral epi basal, oral basal/suprabasal cells; Oral epi krt, oral keratinocytes; PN, postnatal; PreAM, preameloblasts; Secretory AM, secretory ameloblasts; SI/SR, stratum intermedium/stellate reticulum.

sec.p: A distinct oral epithelial subtype expressing KRT6A and KRT13 was termed oral keratinocytes (Oral epi krt). Cluster 1, characterized by BMI1, ASCL2, and TFCP2L1, was identified as oral progenitor cells. Additional subpopulations included preameloblasts (PreAM, expressing VWDE), enamel knot cells (EK, expressing SHH, WNT10B, LEF1, BMP4), inner enamel epithelial cells (IEE, expressing EPHA7), secretory ameloblasts (Secretory AM, expressing AMELX), stratum intermedium/stellate reticulum cells (SI/SR, expressing CYGB, SOX5, CDH12, IGFBP5), and outer enamel epithelial cells (OEE, expressing KRT15). The localization of SOX5 and KRT15 was confirmed via immunohistochemistry (Figure S2A).

While both dental and oral epithelial cells shared core epithelial markers (eg, KRT5 and KRT14), Dental epi cells were distinguished by high expression of SCUBE3 and MPPED1, whereas oral epithelial cells expressed KRT6A, KRT13, ELF5, MEIS2, PLD1 and KRTDAP (Figure 2C,D). Correlation analysis revealed similarities between EK and PreAM cells, Denal epi and OEE cells, as well as Oral epi basal and Oral epi krt cells (Figure S2B).

Cell deconvolution analysis enabled spatial mapping of each epithelial subpopulation (Figure 2E). IEE, OEE, and SI/SR cells were appropriately located within the dental epithelium. PreAM and EK cells were positioned beneath Dental epi cells. Oral progenitors were diffusely distributed in gingival regions, consistent with their high abundance (Figure 2F). The epithelial subtypes became less abundant over time, and ameloblasts were not detected before PCW15.

Cell cycle and regulatory network analyses showed the molecular characteristics of epithelial subtypes. Oral epi basal cells had high proliferative activity, with a large fraction in the S phase. In contrast, Secretory AM and Oral epi krt cells were largely in M/G1 phase, indicating terminal differentiation (Figure 2G). BHLHE40 in Oral epi basal cells, ELF3 in Oral epi krt cells, NR2C2 in OEE, and HMGA2 in IEE were validated using spatial RNA-seq (Figure 2H and Figure S2C).

To ensure reliability, DEGs were analysed using a pseudobulk strategy.13 The representative DEGs across odontogenic epithelial subtypes are listed in Table 1 and Table S2. Cross-referencing the top 100 DEGs with mouse odontogenic datasets helped identify conserved markers (Table S3). Genes shown in Figure 2I and Table S4 were validated across at least one other dataset, offering candidate markers for cross-species identification of odontogenic cells.14, 15, 16, 17 Pearson correlation analysis between human and mouse epithelial subtypes revealed notable similarities, particularly among oral progenitors, Dental epi, SI/SR, and ameloblasts (Figure 2J and Figure S2D).

sec.p: We further explored the differentiation trajectories of odontogenic epithelial cells. A real-time cell density map identified two lineage origins: Dental epi as the progenitor for dental lineage, and Oral epi basal cells for oral epithelium (Figure 3A). Entropy analysis indicated higher differentiation potential in both progenitor groups18 (Figure 3B). Using Monocle3 and RNA velocity, we defined four trajectories: (1) Dental epi to PreAM and ameloblasts; (2) Dental epi to OEE; (3) Dental epi to SI/SR; and (4) Oral epi basal to Oral epi krt, representing oral keratinization (Figure 3A,C). Table 2 lists the top 10 genes altered along each path. TFs likely regulating dental trajectories included TSHZ3, CSRNP3, GLI3, NPAS3 and BNC2, while EHF, BARX2, GRHL1, OVOL1, FOXN1 and ELF3 were implicated in oral epithelial differentiation (Figure 3D).

caption.p: Differentiation trajectories of odontogenic epithelial cells. (A) Real-time visualization of epithelial cell lineage trajectories using Monocle3. Black circles indicate starting points; white circles indicate trajectory branches. Top: Ameloblast (①→②→③), OEE (①→④), SI/SR (①→⑤). Bottom: Keratinization (①→③). (B) Single-cell entropy analysis showing differentiation potential across subpopulations. (C) RNA velocity analysis depicting directionality of cell transitions. (D) Expression levels of transcription factors associated with dental and oral epithelial differentiation.
The top 10 significantly altered genes linked to epithelial differentiation trajectories.

sec.p: Pseudotime analysis further revealed that genes involved in ganglioside metabolism and cell proliferation were enriched along the OEE trajectory. Genes linked to cell junction assembly were prominent in the SI/SR trajectory, while neuron projection morphogenesis and cytoskeletal organization were enriched in the ameloblast lineage (Figure S3). These findings align well with current models of dental epithelial development.

sec.title: Molecular characteristics of odontogenic mesenchymal cells from the cap to early bell stage
sec.p: To investigate the heterogeneity of odontogenic mesenchymal cells, we focused on MSX1+/PRRX1+ cells. Following data normalization, cell cycle regression, batch correction, dimensionality reduction, and clustering, nine distinct mesenchymal subpopulations were identified (Figure 4A,B, Table S1). Among these, dental pulp cells (DP) were marked by the expression of SOX5, FGF3, and FGF10. A subset of DP cells showing high expression of cell cycle-related genes (TOP2A, MKI67, CDK1) was classified as proliferative dental pulp cells (Cycling DP). Dental follicle cells (DF) were identified by EPHA3 expression. Cells expressing TNC, SP7, RUNX2 and RARRES1 were labelled as early odontoblasts (OD early), while another subpopulation, expressing genes associated with mature odontoblasts – S100A13, DSPP, DMP1 and SPARC – was defined as late odontoblasts/osteoblasts (OD late/OB). Due to a limited number of osteoblasts in this group, they were not separately classified.

(D) Proportions of mesenchymal subpopulations across developmental stages. (E) Cell cycle distribution in mesenchymal subpopulations. (F) Transcription factors enriched in each mesenchymal subtype. (G) Real-time cell density and differentiation trajectories of mesenchymal cells. Black circle: starting point; white circles: trajectories – ① odontoblast, ② osteoblast, ③ LGR5+ Msc self-renewal. (H) Heatmap showing pseudotime gene expression changes and enriched pathways along odontoblast differentiation. sec.p: Cranial neural-crest cells (CNCC) were identified by high levels of TFAP2B and LHX6, along with the neural differentiation marker S100B.19 Spatial deconvolution analysis confirmed the localization of these subpopulations (Figure 4C). DF cells were primarily distributed around the tooth germ; Cycling DP cells were enriched in the apical region of the dental papilla, while DP cells were more broadly dispersed throughout the papilla. These distributions were further validated through immunohistochemistry (Figure S4A). Notably, OD late/OB cells were observed in bone-forming regions at PCW12, providing additional confirmation of our annotations.

We also identified mesenchymal progenitor cells (Msc progenitors), characterized by PRRX1, TRPS1 and NANOG expression. Other subtypes included COL3A1+ mesenchymal cells (COL3A1+ Msc) and LGR5+ mesenchymal cells (LGR5+ Msc). LGR5+ Msc cells expressed markers associated with stemness, including LGR5, MCAM, SOX2, and CD24. Spatial analysis revealed that these cells were scattered in the gingival tissues, particularly near the dental follicle and bone regions. Their distribution in the dental papilla and periodontal tissues was confirmed by LGR5 immunostaining (Figure S4B). Since Lgr5-overexpressing mesenchymal stem cells exhibited increased osteogenic capacity, these LGR5+ Msc cells are likely involved in osteogenic/odontogenic differentiation.20

COL3A1+ Msc cells displayed fewer highly variable genes – such as COL3A1, COL6A2, VIM, ACTG1 and IGFBP5 – which were enriched for neuron projection development and biomineral tissue development (Figure S4C,D). These cells were located near the periodontal region. RNA velocity analysis showed a lack of outward vector projection in COL3A1+ Msc cells, suggesting a stable transcriptional state rather than a transitional phase between progenitor and differentiated cells21 (Figure S4E).

During the cap-to-early bell stage, the proportion of DP cells increased progressively, while the proportions of progenitor mesenchymal populations, including Msc progenitors and LGR5+ Msc cells, decreased (Figure 4D). Cell cycle analysis revealed that most Cycling DP cells were in the S and G2/M phases, indicating high proliferative activity. In contrast, DF cells were largely in the G1 phase (Figure 4E), while the other mesenchymal subtypes showed no marked differences in cell cycle distribution.

TF analysis identified the top five TFs enriched in each mesenchymal subpopulation (Figure 4F). GABPB1, NFIC, and TCF4 were upregulated in DP cells, whereas MYBL2 was particularly enriched in Cycling DP cells. DF cells exhibited strong expression of NR2C2. The spatial expression of these TFs was supported by spatial transcriptomics data (Figure S4F).

To further compare with existing models, we performed Pearson correlation analysis between human and mouse datasets. LGR5+ Msc and COL3A1+ Msc cells showed notable transcriptional similarity to mouse mesenchymal cell types, including dental follicle and dental pulp cells (Figure S4G). Using pseudobulk analysis, we identified the representative DEGs among odontogenic mesenchymal subpopulations (Table 3 and Table S5). Common DEGs conserved across both human and mouse datasets are presented in Table S3, offering promising markers for identifying odontogenic mesenchymal cells across species.

sec.p: We next examined the differentiation trajectories of these mesenchymal cells. Based on cell density mapping and RNA velocity, LGR5+ Msc cells were identified as the origin of the odontoblast lineage (Figure 4G and Figure S4E). And the driver genes involving in mesenchymal differentiation were listed (Table S6). Along the pseudotime trajectory, genes inhibiting WNT signalling – such as DKK2 and PRICKLE1 – showed progressive downregulation, highlighting the critical role of WNT signalling in odontoblast differentiation.22,23 Simultaneously, ossification-related genes (SPP1, DMP1, RUNX2, TNC) were increasingly expressed, indicating ongoing mineralization during odontoblast maturation (Figure 4H).

We then applied SCENIC to identify TF regulating these transitions. RARB, TCF4, and ETV1 were predicted to control the upregulated genes along the odontoblast differentiation trajectory, while TWIST1 was associated with downregulated genes. Expression patterns of these TFs aligned with their inferred functions: RARB, TCF4, and ETV1 were elevated in differentiating OD cells, while TWIST1 expression declined (Figure 4I).

sec.title: Cell–cell communication in the periodontal microenvironment
sec.p: To gain a more comprehensive understanding of intercellular interactions during tooth development, we applied CellChat to analyse the signalling communications among key cell types within the periodontal microenvironment. Our initial focus was on the interactions between odontogenic epithelial and mesenchymal cells, which revealed varying signal intensities across cell types (Figure S5A-C). From PCW12 to PCW18, several signalling pathways – including FGF, NRG, PTN, SEMA3, PDGF and PTH – were predominantly secreted by epithelial cells toward mesenchymal cells (Figure 5A). Conversely, pathways such as BMP, ACTIVIN, NRG, FGF, MDK, PTN, PERIOSTIN, and SPP1 were transmitted from mesenchymal to epithelial cells (Figure 5B).

caption.p: Cell–cell communication networks in the periodontal microenvironment. (A and B) Comparison of prominent L-R pairs between epithelial and mesenchymal cells across PCW12, PCW15, and PCW18. (C) Dot plot showing significant L-R interactions between epithelial and mesenchymal cell types. (D and F) Spatial proximity analysis between SPP1⁺ macrophages, general macrophages, and neighbouring cell types using CellTrek. (E, G, H) Inferred signalling pathways between macrophages, mesenchymal, and vascular-related cell types in the periodontal microenvironment. Endo lymph, lymphatic endothelial cells; Endo vessel, vascular endothelial cells; SPP1+ Macro, SPP1+ macrophages; VSMC/PC, vascular smooth muscle cells and pericytes.

sec.p: Among the most commonly expressed ligand-receptor (L-R) pairs were MDK-LRP1, FGF10-FGFR1/FGFR2, and BMP7-BMPR1A/BMPR2. These pairs were not only identified through CellChat but also validated through spatial transcriptomic visualization (Figure S5D). Specifically, the FGF10-FGFR2 pair was enriched in the dental follicle and periodontal regions, while BMP7-BMPR1A and MDK-LRP1 were broadly distributed across both odontogenic mesenchyme and epithelium. Immunohistochemical analysis further confirmed the colocalization of BMP7 and BMPR1A in the apical papilla and periodontal mesenchymal tissues (Figure S5E).

We next examined the distribution of key developmental signalling pathways – including Hedgehog (HH), WNT, BMP, FGF, TGFβ – across epithelial and mesenchymal subpopulations. EK and PreAM cells were the primary source of SHH and FGF9 ligands among epithelial subtypes, while their corresponding receptors, PTCH and FGFR, were widely expressed in mesenchymal cells (Figure 5C). Mesenchymal subpopulations expressed a variety of ligands from the FGF (FGF7/10), BMP (BMP2/5/6/7), WNT (WNT5B), and TGFβ (TGFB1/2/3) families.

Recognizing the importance of the broader periodontal microenvironment, we next analysed nonodontogenic cell populations including endothelial cells, pericytes, Schwann cells, and immune cells.24 Using established markers, PTPRC+ immune cells were subdivided into CD68+/CD163+/CD86+ macrophages (Macrophages), CD68+/SPP1+ macrophages (SPP1+ Macro), and CD14+/APOE+ monocytes (Figure S5F). Vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMC) and pericytes (PC) were grouped as VSMC/PC cells based on shared expression of ACTA2, MYH11, and RGS5. PECAM1+/VWF+ endothelial cells were further classified into vascular endothelial cells (Endo vessel) and lymphatic endothelial cells (Endo lymph), based on markers such as CDH5, CD93, CD34 (vascular) and CCL21, PROX1, LYVE1, MMRN1 (lymphatic) (Figure S5G).

To evaluate potential interactions between these populations and odontogenic cells, spatial proximity was assessed using CellTrek. Notably, SPP1+ macrophages were found in closest spatial proximity to early and late-stage odontoblasts (OD early and OD late/OB) (Figure 5D). Communication analysis showed that SPP1+ macrophages predominantly signalled to OD early cells via SPP1 ligand and integrin receptors (Figure 5E), while a smaller subset of signals, including PTN, SPP1 and FGF10, targeted OD late/OB cells.

Macrophages were also frequently located near VSMC/PC, vascular endothelial, and Schwann cells (Figure 5F). These interactions were mediated through signalling pathways involving NAMPT, SPP1, and VEGFA (Figure 5G). Spatial analysis further revealed that VSMC/PC and Schwann cells were positioned close to DF and OD cells (Figure S5H). VSMC/PC cells communicated with DF and OD cells through POSTN, MDK, NRG3, FGF2, PTN, and SEMA3C signals. Meanwhile, Schwann cells contributed to the signalling landscape via SEMA3C, MDK, and PDGFC (Figure 5H).

Collectively, these findings highlight the dynamic and multidirectional signalling activity between periodontal and odontogenic mesenchymal cells. This complexity underscores the need for further exploration into how the periodontal microenvironment shapes dental development.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Human tooth development begins around PCW6 and progresses through the bud, cap, and bell stages. During this process, dentin- and enamel-producing cells undergo significant morphological changes and begin secreting extracellular matrices that eventually mineralize into dentin and enamel.25 While previous studies, including those by Alghadeer et al and Shi et al, have characterized human embryonic teeth using snRNA-seq and spatial RNA-seq at later stages (PCW12-24), the earlier embryonic phases remain less well characterized due to the difficulty in obtaining sufficient numbers of odontogenic cells at these timepoints.

In this study, we integrated single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomic data to construct high-resolution cellular maps of human embryonic tooth germs between PCW12 and PCW18. Our analysis revealed spatial-temporal expression patterns and cell differentiation trajectories. Furthermore, we explored intercellular signalling within the periodontal microenvironment, including interactions between odontogenic epithelial and mesenchymal cells, as well as endothelial cells, macrophages, and Schwann cells. Understanding diverse cell types enhances selecting optimal cells for regenerative applications, while identifying genes activated/repressed during lineage differentiation may facilitate novel tooth regeneration therapies – for instance, we identified TNC as a top mesenchymal differentiation driver, consistent with its validated role in odontoblastic differentiation of dental pulp stem cells.26 These driver genes and stemness-associated markers represent promising targets to manipulate regenerative capacity, though underlying mechanisms and genetic pathways require further study, guiding efforts to improve tooth regeneration strategies.

Due to the scarcity of embryonic dental tissues from individual donors, we obtained sufficient cell numbers by sampling from multiple donors at each developmental stage.27 However, interindividual variability and differences in developmental age posed challenges for precise temporal alignment. While the differentiation trajectory of odontogenic epithelial cells appeared relatively linear, mesenchymal differentiation was more complex, with multiple potential origins. In particular, we focused on odontoblast lineage commitment and investigated the expression dynamics of key genes and TF along this trajectory. Prior studies have implicated TF such as TCF4 and TWIST1 in odontoblast development; herein, we identified a set of odontogenic driver genes, including TNC, SFRP4, CAPZB, ASPM, COL1A2, DFFA, ENO1, FAT3, NDC1, CLSTN1, MEGF6, GNC1, and PGK1. The upregulated expression of the proteins encoded by these genes were also observed via label-free proteomics from PCW12 to PCW18.28 The proteomic data provide evidential support for the findings of our single-cell analysis.

Epithelial-mesenchymal interactions are central to oral and craniofacial development, mediated by classical signalling pathways such as TGF-β, WNT, FGF, HH, and NOTCH.29 Our study found that, in addition to these well-known pathways, molecules such as MK, PTN, NRG, SEMA3, and POSTN also contribute significantly to epithelial-mesenchymal signalling. This is consistent with findings in other organ systems – such as the hair follicle, limb, and gut – which share developmental similarities with the tooth germ.30, 31, 32

For instance, odontogenic epithelial cells expressed HH ligands, including the Frizzled coreceptor LRP5, similar to intestinal epithelium.32 Meanwhile, mesenchymal cells expressed high levels of TGF-β ligands (BMP2, BMP5) and noncanonical WNT signals (WNT5A). FGF8 and FGF10, known to mediate epithelial-mesenchymal crosstalk during limb development via FGFR2, were also colocalized in the developing tooth.31 The spatial overlap of FGF8/10 and FGFR2 expression in dental tissues highlights FGFR2’s potential role in coordinating dental morphogenesis (Figure S5D). Similarly, robust BMP7 signalling observed here aligns with its known involvement in both tooth and hair follicle development.30

Periodontal cells, which form the structural foundation of the maxillofacial region, also play a crucial role in shaping dental development.33 In our study, we identified a population of SPP1+ macrophages in close spatial proximity to early and late-stage odontoblasts. These macrophages appeared to communicate with odontoblasts via the SPP1-ITGAV interaction. Previous studies have shown that soluble SPP1 promotes osteogenic differentiation, supporting the hypothesis that SPP1+ macrophages may influence odontoblast maturation.34 Furthermore, pericytes were predicted to interact with DF and OD cells through POSTN-ITGAV_ITGB5 and MDK-LRP1 interactions. Schwann cells were contributed to the microenvironment through SEMA3C signalling, known to mediate axon guidance and potentially influence dental innervation.35 Since glial cell derivatives and pericytes can differentiate into odontoblasts, dental pulp cells, and other cell types, regulating these signalling pathways can also guide the behaviour of odontogenic stem cells, which is worthy of further exploration.36

However, this study focused on a relatively narrow developmental timepoints and small sample sizes. Additionally, the relatively low spatial resolution of each spot complicates the integration of omics data and imaging. Although we applied deconvolution methods to analyse spatial transcriptomic data, the presence of multiple cells within a single spot may reduce the accuracy of cell localization, necessitating further in situ RNA or protein hybridization for precise cell mapping. Future research should expand to additional timepoints with repeated sampling, and the genes identified in this study still require cross-validation in postnatal samples.

Furthermore, our current analyses combined molar and incisor tissues. While this approach provided sufficient data for general developmental mapping, it limited our ability to distinguish between tooth types. A recent study by Wang et al37 on mouse embryonic teeth highlighted key transcriptional differences between incisors and molars, particularly within mesenchymal cells. In our dataset, known incisor markers (ALX1, ALX3, HAND1) and molar markers (TBX15, LHX6) were also differentially expressed in mesenchymal populations. However, it remains unclear whether these mouse-derived markers can reliably differentiate human tooth types, underscoring the need for further investigation to identify human-specific markers.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Our study presents a detailed spatial-temporal map of human embryonic tooth development from the cap to early bell stage, identifying key gene signatures associated with odontogenic cell differentiation. This enriches the transcriptomic resources in tooth germ development research. Additionally, through the integration of single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomic analyses, we identified cell communication between epithelial cells, mesenchymal cells, macrophages, Schwann cells, pericytes, and adjacent cells. As spatial transcriptomic techniques continue to evolve, higher-resolution mapping and integration with multiomics approaches will further refine our understanding of human tooth development.
